narrative:
Based on the assessment, there is a 22% chance you will fail your final year. While this may not seem high, it exceeds the 10% threshold that triggers the requirement for remedial courses — a precautionary measure designed to support students before difficulties become serious.

The most influential factor in your assessment actually works in your favour: you have no history of past academic failures, which strongly suggests you have the capability to succeed. Similarly, your ambition to pursue higher education is a positive signal — and notably, every single student not required to take remedial courses also shares this goal, so you are in good company there.

However, the factor pushing your risk upward is your father's level of education, which is at primary level. Among students not required to take remedial courses, nearly a quarter have fathers with higher education and almost half have fathers with secondary or vocational qualifications. Research consistently shows that parental education influences the kind of academic guidance and support available at home, and this appears to be a contributing factor in your case.

Adding to this concern, your weekly study time is under two hours, whereas students not required to take remedial courses typically study between two and ten hours per week. You also lack internet access at home, which limits your ability to research and study independently.

The remedial courses are therefore an opportunity, not a punishment. Attending them will help compensate for gaps in home-based academic support and encourage stronger study habits — giving you the best possible chance of finishing your final year successfully.
